I'm Neelam, Gargi's roommate, and for five weeks I've watched her "almost start" her internship application essay.
First she read every past winner's essay she could find. Then she made a colour-coded spreadsheet of their structures. Then she bought a book on persuasive writing and underlined half of it. Her outline is taped to our wall, and every night she moves the sticky notes around.
Yesterday I asked, "How much have you written?"
"Nothing yet, but the structure's nearly perfect." She sounded proud, even cheerful.
But when I offered to read a rough paragraph, she went very still. "Not until it's ready. I don't want anyone seeing a bad version."
I can't know what's going on in her head. From outside, it looks as if she's working all the time.
The deadline is Sunday.

qa.q: What did Gargi make after reading past winners' essays?
qa.a: A colour-coded spreadsheet of their structures.

qa.q: What does Gargi's 'I don't want anyone seeing a bad version' suggest about her preparation?
qa.a: It suggests the preparing protects her from being judged; as long as she is outlining, no one can see a flawed draft.

qa.q: What could help Gargi move from outline to essay before Sunday?
qa.a: She could write one rough paragraph against a short timer and let Neelam read it, to see that a bad version isn't a disaster.

His resume was on version fourteen, in a folder called FINAL_FINAL. Each time he opened the portal, something looked wrong: a weak bullet point, his project described too plainly, a font that suddenly seemed childish. He would close the tab and promise himself the next company.

Dear Zubin Sir,
I owe you an honest email. The Young Writers Fellowship closed at midnight yesterday, and I didn't submit.
You read my story in August and said it was nearly ready. For two months I carried that "nearly" around like a stone. Every weekend I opened the file to send it and saw a clumsy sentence in paragraph two, or an ending that felt too neat, and closed it again. I told myself I'd submit when it was right.
At 11:40 last night I had the form open. I couldn't press the button. Not sending felt safer. If I didn't send it, nobody could reject it.
This morning I woke up and realised I had rejected it myself, before anyone else could. The result is the same; only I chose it.
I'm embarrassed to tell you this. But I didn't want to hide it.
Ritu

Vishal from art school got his first gallery show. I saw the poster today, then went and looked at his work online, and I'm still sitting with it.

Mahima, you asked on the show how I actually got unstuck. Honestly? Tiny experiments.
I'm Deepak, I design app screens, and for two years I didn't share anything until it was pixel-perfect. So my counsellor suggested one rule: set a timer, make something rough, show one trusted person, and write down what happens.

Second week, I showed a messy prototype in a team meeting. My manager asked a question, I answered, the meeting moved on.

Trisha, you're sulking because your Kathak footwork feels stuck? Sit. Let your Ojas Tauji tell you about a typewriter.
When I was fifteen, in Kanpur, Babuji sent me to Sharma-ji's typing institute so I could get a clerk's job one day. In the first month I went from nothing to twenty-five words a minute. I thought I'd be a champion by summer. Then I reached thirty, and there I stayed. Two whole months. Thirty, thirty, thirty.
I told Babuji I had no talent for it and wanted to stop. Sharma-ji, a strict old man, pulled out my test sheets from the first month and from the last week. Yes, my speed was the same. But my errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two. "Your hands learned something your stopwatch couldn't see," he said.
The next month I jumped to forty.
So, beta, your feet are learning something too. You just can't see it yet.

qa.q: What speed did Ojas get stuck at for two months?
qa.a: Thirty words a minute.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell Babuji he had no talent for typing?
qa.a: His speed stayed at thirty for two months, so he believed he had reached his limit.

qa.q: How did Sharma-ji reveal the hidden progress, and what could Trisha try?
qa.a: He compared early and recent test sheets, showing errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two; Trisha could compare old and new Kathak recordings to spot hidden gains in the footwork.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel hearing Tauji's typewriter story?
qa.a: Trisha may feel less alone and more hopeful that the stuck footwork is still improving under the surface.

grounding: Illustrates, through an uncle's memory of a typing plateau, how progress can continue beneath the surface when no visible change shows.
